evidence.source:
Claimed at 0.9 BEFORE looking at the data. If the interval excludes 0.9 the
prediction was wrong, in whichever direction. A verdict is about the prediction
and not about whether the proxy is any good.

relationships.why: claimed 0.9 lies OUTSIDE the 95% CI [0.912, 0.959] for r = 0.936, resampling 10 batch(s)

evidence.source:
Claimed at 0.0 and REQUIRED to hold. Noise must not correlate with the
measurement. If this is refuted the construction is broken and R1 cannot be
read, whichever way R1 went. It also shows how much room ten batches buys: the
width of this interval is the smallest correlation this design can tell from
nothing.

relationships.why: claimed 0.0 lies within the 95% CI [-0.004, 0.303] for r = 0.157, resampling 10 batch(s)

evidence.source:
A sign test, the value claim that carries a p. Each batch contributes one sign,
the majority over its ten samples, and the estimate is the share of batches in
which the proxy over-reads. Claimed at 0.5 and REQUIRED to hold: the noise is
symmetric, so a batch is as likely to over-read as under-read. The row carries
the exact two-sided binomial p against 0.5 beside the interval; on ten batches
the interval is wide, and its width is what a claim such as "the proxy
over-reads in most batches" would have to beat.

relationships.unit_value: the majority sign over a unit's rows (up to 10 rows per unit); equal counts make the unit a tie and it is dropped
relationships.p_method: exact two-sided binomial against 0.5 over 8 batch(s)
relationships.why: claimed 0.5 lies within the 95% CI [0.375, 1] for sign_test = 0.75 (6 of 8 batch(s) are the event, exact two-sided binomial p = 0.289 against 0.5), resampling 8 batch(s)
